states.cards:
The data support
Ontario's long-term share peaked at 72.9% in 2021 Q3 with about as many long-term cases as in 2019 Q4 (130,096 vs 130,444) but fewer cases overall.
In the latest quarter (2026 Q1), the highest shares were in Peterborough, St. Catharines–Niagara, London; the lowest in Guelph, Barrie (Ontario: 50.1%).
Barrie, Guelph and Brantford had a lower long-term share than Ontario in at least 90% of quarters.
Rankings shift: Toronto ranked 1 of 15 before the pandemic and 14 of 15 after it.
Across the 15 CMAs, the rank correlation between the unemployment rate and the long-term share was +0.44 before, +0.14 during and −0.44 after the pandemic (before = 2011 Q1 – 2019 Q4, when unemployment data exist).
The data do not show
Why the total caseload fell in 2020–2021, or why it grew afterwards.
How long a new case will last, or how likely any person is to stay on assistance.
That a CMA's local services or policies caused its higher or lower share.
That local unemployment explains or causes a CMA's long-term share: the unemployment rate counts people in the labour market, not OW cases, and is background only.
Regional differences in need: a share of the caseload is not a rate per population.
Worth investigating
Above Ontario before, during and after the pandemic: Peterborough and Oshawa (in at least one period by under 2 pp).
Large rank changes, such as Toronto, before reading any single quarter's ranking as stable.
Why the Ontario long-term share has risen again since 2024 Q4 (compare with case counts in Figure 1a).
Why Peterborough had the highest long-term share after the pandemic (59.0%) while its unemployment rate ranked 13 of 15 (5.8%; Figure 5a).

states.cards:
The data support
Ontario's long-term share peaked at 72.9% in 2021 Q3 with about as many long-term cases as in 2019 Q4 (130,096 vs 130,444) but fewer cases overall.
In the selected period (2005 Q1 – 2009 Q4), the highest shares were in Toronto, Ottawa–Gatineau, Windsor; the lowest in Guelph, Barrie (Ontario: 31.0%).
Barrie, Guelph and Brantford had a lower long-term share than Ontario in at least 90% of quarters.
Rankings shift: Toronto ranked 1 of 15 before the pandemic and 14 of 15 after it.
Across the 15 CMAs, the rank correlation between the unemployment rate and the long-term share was +0.44 before, +0.14 during and −0.44 after the pandemic (before = 2011 Q1 – 2019 Q4, when unemployment data exist).
The data do not show
Why the total caseload fell in 2020–2021, or why it grew afterwards.
How long a new case will last, or how likely any person is to stay on assistance.
That a CMA's local services or policies caused its higher or lower share.
That local unemployment explains or causes a CMA's long-term share: the unemployment rate counts people in the labour market, not OW cases, and is background only.
Regional differences in need: a share of the caseload is not a rate per population.
Worth investigating
Above Ontario before, during and after the pandemic: Peterborough and Oshawa (in at least one period by under 2 pp).
Large rank changes, such as Toronto, before reading any single quarter's ranking as stable.
Why the Ontario long-term share has risen again since 2024 Q4 (compare with case counts in Figure 1a).
Why Peterborough had the highest long-term share after the pandemic (59.0%) while its unemployment rate ranked 13 of 15 (5.8%; Figure 5a).
